hook.text: Opower sends energy reports comparing your usage to neighbors. Households receiving them cut energy by 2%.

buildup.text: Peer comparison taps into competitive instinct and social conformity. Nobody wants to be the worst on the block.

discovery.text: Allcott's study found that Opower's social comparison nudge is equivalent to a 20% price increase in reducing.

twist.text: The effect fades over time but doesn't disappear. Persistent reminders keep the comparison salient and behavior.

climax.text: Peer comparison works for water, energy, taxes, and even antibiotics prescribing.

punchline.text: Nobody wants to be the outlier. Use that.

quiz.question: What effect did Opower's peer comparison have?
options: No measurable change in energy use
A 2% energy reduction, equivalent to a 20% price increase
People used more energy to outdo neighbors

details.summary: Peer comparison nudges show individuals how their behavior compares to similar others. Home energy reports that compare your usage to your neighbors', fitness apps that show peer activity levels, and tax compliance letters that cite community rates all leverage social comparison.
details.whyItMatters: Peer comparison is one of the most cost-effective behavior change tools available. Energy comparison programs alone save billions of kilowatt-hours annually.
takeaways: Showing people how they compare to peers shifts behavior toward the norm
Energy comparison programs save billions of kilowatt-hours annually at low cost
The most effective comparisons use similar peers rather than abstract averages

faq.question: How do home energy report nudges work?
faq.answer: Utility companies send reports comparing a household's energy use to similar neighbors. Homes using more than average receive a message showing the gap with suggestions for reduction. This peer comparison consistently reduces energy consumption by 1 to 3 percent.

faq.question: Can peer comparison nudges have negative effects?
faq.answer: Yes, the boomerang effect occurs when below-average users learn the norm and increase their consumption. Adding injunctive signals like smiley faces for below-average users prevents this. Poorly designed comparisons can also trigger resentment or disengagement.
